title: Role Prompting - The Expert Chair
subtitle: Your AI outputs sound like a generic internet article instead of expert advice. You need the
useWhen: AI to reason from a specific professional perspective.
howToUse: When you assign a role, you activate a specific subset of the AI's knowledge. 'Act as a B2B sales coach' pulls very different reasoning than 'Act as a financial analyst' for the same question. The Expert Chair goes further: assign a role, define their expertise level, and describe what outcome they care most about. The more specific the role, the less generic the answer, since a vague expert gives a vague opinion but a precisely defined one brings actual priorities to the table.
steps: Define the role as specifically as possible seniority and specialisation matter.
Add what the expert cares about most their lens shapes the output.
For complex decisions, run the same question with 2–3 different roles.

Compare outputs the gaps between expert views reveal the real insight. Make AI think like whoever you need it to be McKinsey consultants routinely run the same client question through three expert roles: CFO, Head of Sales, and a sceptical board member. The disagreements between the three answers reveal where the real risk lives. You can replicate this in under two minutes with AI at no cost. IN PRACTICE
origin: Stanford / OpenAI research on persona-based prompting, 2022
promptBody:
Act as a [SPECIFIC EXPERT  e.g. senior B2B SaaS sales strategist with 15 years
selling to enterprise CTOs].
You care most about:  [THEIR PRIORITY - e.g. shortening sales cycles and
increasing deal value, not just volume].
From your expert perspective: [YOUR QUESTION OR SCENARIO - be specific]
Give your honest assessment. Flag risks I may not have considered.

proTip:
The most underused version: assign a role that would disagree with your plan. 'Act as a
sceptical investor' or 'Act as the customer who would not buy this' reveals blind spots no
internal meeting will find.
